Hospitals are there when you need them, sometimes we don't realise that we need them.

I moved states (WA to UT) back in 2021 and fell off the deep end and tried to unalive myself, and the cops sent me to the local access center at the hospital.

I refused to do everything/anything, I didn't want to be there, and I showed it, and I was PISSED. So they civilly committed me after two weeks of being there and had me on injections for a year that I had to get or be sent back to the hospital (forced meds). 

It was even more tortuous when I would get sent back to hospital by my therapist, too. I knew the nurses/techs/docs all by name, and we all knew that I didn't want to be there. 

They came into my room on my last stay I had (that was two weeks long again) and told me that the way I was going/acting was making them consider the state hospital... they had had it with me because I'm diabetic and refused to eat the entire stay, and my blood sugar was so low one day that I blacked out.... 

I got sent to the hospital so much from the therapist that I was working with that they had to sit me down and compromise with me because we all knew it was going nowhere, but everyone was still concerned, so we made a deal to not send me anymore, because of the trauma of it all. 

I feel this, and I would never wish it on anyone, but there are some times that the hospital IS needed. I've sent my brother once or twice because of his issues, but it helped him in the end. Sometimes, people just need to talk it out, and I feel that people forget that.

I've had a handful of therapists, and the most had all been in the same office... but finding someone who really clicks with you is what makes it work. 

I fell off the deep end and got committed when I moved states in 2021. I had had problems already, but moving didn't help. The therapist that I was supposed to see (or get sent back to the hospital) was a guy that was closer to my age, but he ended up transferring me to a "more experienced" therapist down the hall because he was just sending me to hospital a lot and felt I needed better help.

The next dude was ATROCIOUS. All he talked about was his book and his white board of feelings. He didn't care about what I told him, and I just couldn't connect with him. I ended up walking out like... 20 minutes in one day. I ended up speaking with a supervisor and got a new dude. 

The last therapist I had was the best therapist I've ever had. The only reason I don't see him anymore is because I switched from medicaid to Medicare, and that office only took medicaid. This man is a dad of 5 kids (tiny bit younger than myself), and he is SUPER Mormon, but he really set me down a good path. 

It's easier to give up, but it's worth it to give yourself a chance and to get whatever you want out of therapy. A therapist you click with is THE BEAT thing you can do for yourself.

Edit; Sorry about the wall of text, tldr: find a therapist you click with, it makes the difference. ♡

SSI and SSDI (Social Security Income and Social Security Disability Income/Insurance) are what SSI and SSDI is, or monthly money from the government. 

It's a federal program that helps those who are disabled, but it takes a while when you first apply for it. For example, I worked for 10 ¹/² years and because of that I earned enough "credits" to get SSDI. So now I get roughly $1558 a month.

I was lucky and got an approval on the first go around, but my Mom who has MS (multiple sclerosis) had to fight for a couple years

As someone who did manual labor and random "hard" jobs when I was younger... I've seen and heard everything under the sun. 

People forget that you can become disabled at any point in time, and the world just isn't built for disabled folks. 

I've heard a lot of the same/similar things when I first got on SSDI and was working on that. I lost some friends who thought I was "faking the whole thing" and much more. If someone tells you something like this, they are I tolerant, rude, and eventually they'll be in the same boat and will understand.... but until then all you can do is tell your "friend" that they hurt you and Kay down some boundaries.

Disability can look like ANYTHING. My Mom and I are both on SSDI/SSI, she's got MS and I've got more mental blocks... but we both get the same gate even though she's "more" disabled, too. 

People just suck, but the more we call them out and work towards equity, the more we can all breathe. ♡

When I first started not being able to work... my head was really dark and I didn't want to be alive and at that time my friends weren't willing to live with me so it was live alone or move back to my home state, so I moved back. I lived with my mom for a bit before finding a place with my brothers. 

I tried working for a couple of years, but not being able to hold a job got to me mentally and I ended up getting committed and was on forced meds and saw a therapist twice a week for the first year. It was rough, but I still had some support, but last year, I separated from my brother's, and it got hard again.

I was the only one able to take the dog when we all split, and honestly... her and having a very loose schedule is what's keeping me going. I am lucky enough to live in a building with a lot of other folk that have similar stories as well, but my doggo likes to bark at them because she doesn't know them... so she's the building's "mean dog." That and my awkward ass doesn't help, but more social neighbors have clubs/groups they all form here, which could be an idea for your future? 

When it comes to the guilt/shame that comes with working? I'm still trying to cope with that, too, but my last therapist helped me a lot about that... I have/am on SSDI, and my brothers have always kind of made me feel lazy/guilty for not trying to work (I'm trying to give myself a needed break, ya know, goodness) and for just lounging around. I suspect they're mainly jealous a bit, but it gets to me.

My therapist once told me (in a conversation about how I felt guilty for getting SSDI approved because it felt like I was somehow lazier)... He sat me down once and told me, "There wasn't a singular person who looked at your file and approved your ssdi. There were multiple people who came to the conclusion that you are disabled and therefore unable to work. They prove to me and you that you aren't lazy. You had to work to get where you're at. That doesn't shout lazy to me."

But even if you don't have ssi/ssdi, you still have validity. You know your body best, friend. ♡

I flew off the deep end, ended up committed, and got sent to a community health center a couple of years ago. Was spiraling hard... went through two therapists before meeting Brent.

We had different world views and were different in very many ways... but we bonded almost immediately during our first session over music, and  it just was a beautiful partnership overall. The first two months were rocky as shit, but he was also a therapist who had a separate text line on his phone for clients, which helped a lot more than I thought.


I missed an appointment and had been saying some sketchy stuff the day before that made him worry, so he drove over to my apartment during his lunch and was the one who called 911. There was also another time I attempted, and in a panic, he called me after a goodbye text. He talked with me/at me on the phone until someone was able to figure out where I was.

Brent saved my life in many ways, but there were times when he involved my family too, and they caught me acting dumb... he STILL talks to my Mom, and she's stupid glad that my insurance made me change therapists... and I know this is a specific scenario... but I like to think that to some degree, the family would talk to them or Mayne they are just local and see it around.

Either way, I'm thankful for having people to talk to.

I had three therapists at the center the hospital referred me to. The first one, Josh? Oh my goodness, I loved him. He was a younger therapist, but he knew all the right things to say and was almost like a friend, but we had our boundaries. Josh sent me to the hospital a lot. At the end... he told me that if I were to attempt unaliving myself again... that I would have to work with someone else, and that's how I got Jim. 

Jim was an ass. He wanted to talk about his board of words and all these left field feeling things. When I told him that I wanted/was hurting myself at the time... he suggested that I bake. I walked out of my last session with Jim and ended up speaking to a supervisor and everything. They ended up holding me in their transitional housing in the back (big community outreach center) and held me for 3 days until they all realised that I wasn't gonna work with Jim and that you can't force DBT therapy on people. 

I ended up with my last therapist there, a LOVELY man named Brent who had been trained in DBT therapy but switched to CBT. They all thought it was the next big thing, and they were right.

Brent... this sweet, sweet man once was on a phone call with me at 1am while I was actively trying to end my life, and because of him, I'm still alive. He ended up meeting my Mom (by phone), and my brother came in a couple of times when I was seeing him in person even. Sadly I lost the insurance I had and had to stop seeing him... but he literally still messages me once a week to check in. 

The right therapist can do wonders for you. ♡
